Titration. A quantitative chemical analysis method used to determine the unknown concentration of an identified analyte. A reagent of known concentration and volume, called the titrant, is added from a buret to a known volume of the analyte solution until the chemical reaction reaches its equivalence point, which is often detected using a color-changing chemical indicator or a pH meter.

Reaction completion is signaled at the equivalence point, which is visually indicated by the endpoint of a chemical indicator such as phenolphthalein, which turns from colorless to pink in basic conditions. This endpoint displays a sharp vertical inflection on a titration curve, which plots pH for acid-base titrations against the volume of added titrant. The midpoint of the vertical section represents the equivalence point. During the buffer region, prior to the equivalence point of a weak acid titration, the pH can be calculated using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

Beyond traditional acid-base titrations, specialized methods address different analytical challenges. Karl Fischer titration is a specialized redox method that uses coulometric or volumetric techniques to selectively determine trace amounts of water in a sample. Complexometric methods use chelating agents like EDTA, or ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, to determine the concentration of divalent metal ions in solution.

Karl Fischer titration is the gold-standard method for determining trace moisture in organic solvents and products. Sodium hydroxide is a common strong base titrant used to analyze weak and strong acids, while potassium hydrogen phthalate, or KHP, is a widely used primary standard for calibrating base titrants.
